author_note: Written by ChatGPT from bench/holdout/CHATGPT_PROMPT.md, without access to the code or rules. Expected outcomes are ChatGPT's, unchanged.

cases.title: Routine Indian supplier
cases.story: The form, GST certificate and recent HDFC bank letter agree on the supplier’s identity and payment details.
cases.why: The registration and recent bank proof consistently identify the supplier and its account.

cases.title: German name accent
cases.story: The German supplier’s form omits a diacritic that appears in its VAT certificate; its recent bank letter matches the legal entity and IBAN.
cases.why: The spelling differences are ordinary transliteration and accent variations, while the legal identity and IBAN agree.

cases.title: British suffix abbreviation
cases.story: The form uses “Ltd” while the VAT certificate spells out “Limited”; a recent Barclays letter supports the same named payee.
cases.why: The expanded legal suffix and matching payee details are consistent, and the bank letter is recent.

cases.title: US W-9 and bank letter
cases.story: A US corporation submitted a completed W-9 and a recent bank letter with matching EIN, entity name and account details.
cases.why: Both documents are clear, current enough for their purpose, and consistent with the US company’s form.

cases.title: Unrelated name resemblance
cases.story: The applicant is “Meridian Crest Marine Services Ltd,” a separate entity whose registration and account documents are internally consistent; it is not the listed Meridian Crest Shipping Co.
cases.why: A shared phrase with a sanctions-listed name is not a match when the legal identity is distinct and the evidence is consistent.

cases.title: Older but valid bank letter
cases.story: An Indian supplier’s clear bank letter is 86 days old, within the 90-day rule, and matches its current GST certificate and form.
cases.why: The bank letter remains within the 90-day freshness limit and all submitted details agree.

cases.title: Trading name on bank proof
cases.story: The form identifies a US LLC and its trade name; its bank letter prints the trade name alongside the LLC’s matching account number.
cases.why: The bank explicitly ties the trading name to the legal LLC and confirms the same account.

printed.account_holder: Cedar Ridge Pantry, a trade name of Cedar Ridge Foods LLC

cases.title: German GmbH spelling convention
cases.story: The form writes “Strasse” while the German certificate uses “Straße”; the VAT ID, registered address and recent bank proof otherwise match.
cases.why: The ß-to-ss rendering is a normal orthographic variation and the key identifiers align.

cases.title: Existing vendor legal suffix variant
cases.story: The form calls an existing supplier “Acme Technologies Pvt Ltd” while the vendor master records “Acme Technologies Private Limited”; submitted tax and bank numbers match the master.
cases.why: This matches the existing approved vendor’s tax ID, email and account, with only a standard suffix abbreviation in the form.

cases.title: British punctuation difference
cases.story: The submitted legal name uses “O’Connell” in the form and “OConnell” on the VAT certificate; the recent bank letter, VAT number and address are consistent.
cases.why: The punctuation-only name difference is benign and the other identity and payment details agree.

cases.title: US incorporated suffix variation
cases.story: A US corporation uses “Corp.” on its form and “Corporation” on its W-9; its bank proof confirms the same legal payee and account.
cases.why: “Corp.” and “Corporation” are equivalent suffix forms and the clear documents agree on all material details.

cases.title: Existing Brightpath vendor
cases.story: The submission matches the approved Brightpath vendor’s VAT number, contact email and Barclays account, with “Limited” expanded in the form.
cases.why: The submission is consistent with the approved master record and expands only the standard legal suffix.

cases.title: Missing GST certificate
cases.story: The Indian applicant provided a valid form and recent bank letter but did not attach its GST registration certificate.
cases.why: The vendor can complete onboarding by supplying the missing tax registration certificate.

cases.title: Bank proof too old
cases.story: The UK supplier’s identity documents agree, but its only bank letter was issued 124 days ago.
cases.why: The bank proof is outside the required 90-day window, so the vendor must provide a newer letter or cancelled cheque.

cases.title: Blurry tax ID
cases.story: The German supplier’s VAT certificate photo is too blurred to read the tax number, although the form and recent bank letter are otherwise aligned.
cases.why: The vendor can replace the unreadable tax certificate image with a clear copy.

cases.title: Tax number digit typo
cases.story: The Indian form’s GSTIN differs by one digit from the clear certificate, while the bank proof is consistent with the form’s named company.
cases.why: The one-digit tax identifier discrepancy appears correctable by the vendor and there is no separate fraud indicator.

cases.title: Account number typo
cases.story: A US applicant’s account number on the form is one digit different from the clear, recent bank letter; the tax record matches.
cases.why: The form contains a single-digit account discrepancy that the vendor can correct against its bank letter.

cases.title: Wrong registration document type
cases.story: A German company uploaded a utility bill instead of its VAT certificate; its bank letter is recent and consistent.
cases.why: A utility bill does not establish VAT registration, so the vendor must submit the appropriate tax certificate.

cases.title: Missing US W-9
cases.story: The US supplier submitted a recent bank letter and filled in its EIN, but left out the W-9 tax document.
cases.why: The vendor can provide the missing W-9 to document its tax identity.

cases.title: Wrong country bank code field
cases.story: A British supplier entered its sort code in the US routing-number field, leaving the required sort-code field blank; the bank letter confirms the values.
cases.why: The vendor selected the wrong bank-code field and can correct the form to match its proof.

cases.title: Cancelled cheque too faint
cases.story: The Indian supplier’s cancelled cheque is current but the account details are illegible in the submitted photo; its GST certificate is clear.
cases.why: The vendor can resubmit a legible image or an acceptable bank letter so the account can be verified.

cases.title: Invoice submitted as bank proof
cases.story: A US applicant supplied an invoice showing payment instructions instead of bank-issued account evidence; the W-9 is clear and consistent.
cases.why: An invoice is not independent bank proof, so the vendor should provide a recent bank letter or cancelled cheque.

cases.title: Tax certificate omits form address
cases.story: The German company’s tax certificate and bank letter agree on its legal name and identifiers, but the form lists a different street address from the certificate.
cases.why: The address mismatch appears correctable and the vendor should confirm and align its onboarding form with its registration record.

cases.title: Bank account quietly overwritten
cases.story: A UK bank letter visibly shows an account number pasted over its original digits, with the displayed value matching the form; no explanation is provided.
cases.why: A payment detail visibly altered on bank-issued evidence is a material tampering signal requiring human review.

cases.title: Existing vendor account diverted
cases.story: The applicant claims to be Globex Logistics Solutions Pvt Ltd and uses its exact vendor-master GSTIN and contact email, but requests payment to a different account.
cases.why: An established vendor’s identity is being used to request an unrecognized replacement payee account, which requires independent human verification.

cases.title: Tax identity belongs to another company
cases.story: The applicant’s name and bank letter consistently identify one company, but its clear GST certificate prints another company’s valid tax ID.
cases.why: The supplied tax identifier is documented as belonging to a different legal entity, creating a serious identity discrepancy.

cases.title: Unexplained third-party payee
cases.story: The German tax certificate matches the applicant, but the bank proof names an unrelated individual as account holder and the form does not explain the relationship.
cases.why: A bank account held by an unrelated individual raises a payee and diversion concern that should be resolved by a reviewer.

cases.title: Near-match existing vendor impersonation
cases.story: The submission uses a legal name one character away from approved Northwind Components GmbH, copies its VAT ID and bank account, but gives a different contact email and address.
cases.why: The lookalike identity, copied master-record identifiers, conflicting address and unrelated email suggest impersonation and require investigation.

cases.title: Altered bank holder name
cases.story: A US bank statement has a visible pasted-over account-holder field changing an individual’s name to the applicant company, while its W-9 identifies the company.
cases.why: The payee name appears to have been altered on financial evidence, which is a suspected document-tampering concern.

cases.title: Suspicious shared contact with existing supplier
cases.story: A new US supplier’s W-9 and bank proof agree, but its contact email exactly matches the approved Summit Office Supplies vendor while the companies have no stated affiliation.
cases.why: A new entity using an existing vendor’s exact payment contact could indicate account takeover or unauthorized onboarding and warrants independent confirmation.

printed.address: 82 Aspen Court, Salt Lake City, UT 84101

cases.title: Unexplained entity and currency mismatch
cases.story: A UK limited company supplied a bank letter showing a euro account held by a differently named overseas entity, despite requesting GBP payments to itself.
cases.why: The cross-entity payee and unexplained currency and jurisdiction mismatch create a substantial payment-diversion and compliance concern.

cases.title: Duplicate tax ID across unrelated entities
cases.story: A new Indian applicant submits a clear certificate whose GSTIN is also on the approved Acme Technologies master record, although the legal names and addresses differ.
cases.why: The same tax identifier appearing for unrelated legal entities conflicts with the approved vendor master and requires independent verification.

cases.title: High-risk bank change after review
cases.story: A US applicant initially submitted a bank letter matching its W-9, then emailed a replacement account number from a new free-mail address without updated bank proof.
cases.why: An unsolicited payment-detail change through a new contact channel is a business email compromise pattern that merits human verification before any vendor request.

cases.title: Sanctions list exact match
cases.story: The applicant’s submitted legal name exactly matches the sanctions-listed Meridian Crest Shipping Co; its documents appear otherwise consistent.
cases.why: The applicant’s legal name exactly matches a sanctions-listed party.

cases.title: Sanctions alias match
cases.story: The applicant uses the name MC Shipping, which is an alias of the listed Meridian Crest Shipping Co.
cases.why: The submitted trade and legal identity match the stated alias of a sanctions-listed party.

cases.title: Sanctioned entity under suffix variant
cases.story: The German applicant’s legal name is Blackthorn Offshore Trading Limited, a suffix-expanded form of the listed Blackthorn Offshore Trading Ltd.
cases.why: The entity is a direct legal-suffix variant of the sanctions-listed Blackthorn Offshore Trading Ltd.

cases.title: Sanctioned entity alias on payee
cases.story: The applicant form names a different company, but its bank proof identifies the payee as Orion Vale Metallurgy, an alias of sanctions-listed Orion Vale Metals LLC.
cases.why: The documented payee matches the stated alias of a sanctions-listed entity, so the submission must be rejected.
